name: Boudhanath
tagline: The great white stupa at the heart of Tibetan Kathmandu
meta_description: Boudhanath Stupa guide: evening kora, monasteries, butter lamps, thangka studios, entry fee, Losar, best time to visit and where to stay near the stupa.
summary: Boudhanath is a 36 m white stupa 6 km north-east of Thamel and the centre of Tibetan Buddhist life in Nepal. Pilgrims walk clockwise around it from dawn to dark, dozens of monasteries fill the lanes behind, and the rooftop cafes around the square are the best place in Kathmandu to watch the evening kora.
intro: Few places in Kathmandu change mood as completely as Boudhanath. Step through the gate off the noisy Boudha road and you enter a circular square around one of the largest stupas in Asia: a whitewashed dome on three stepped terraces, a gilded tower painted with the watchful eyes of the Buddha, and strings of prayer flags running from the spire to the rooftops. Tibetan tradition calls it Jarung Khashor and dates it to around the fifth or sixth century, and it is one of the seven monument zones of the Kathmandu Valley World Heritage Site.

After 1959, Tibetan refugees settled around the stupa and built monasteries of every major school, so Boudha is now a working neighbourhood of monks, nuns, thangka painters, incense makers and families who walk the kora every day. More than 50 gompas stand within walking distance, from the large Shechen Monastery, founded by Dilgo Khyentse Rinpoche, to small family shrines up a staircase. The 2015 earthquake cracked the tower, which was taken down and rebuilt by the community, and the stupa was reconsecrated in November 2016.

The rhythm of the day is the reason to come. At 6 am elderly Tibetans are already circling with prayer beads and wheels. By noon the square is quieter, with tour groups and pigeons. From about 5 pm the kora thickens again as monks, families and visitors walk clockwise together in the fading light while butter lamps flicker in the lamp houses. Foreign visitors pay an entry fee of around NPR 400 at the gates, with lower rates for SAARC nationals; check current status before you travel.

highlights.title: Walking the kora at dusk
highlights.text: From around 5 pm the square fills with people circling clockwise: monks in maroon, grandmothers spinning prayer wheels, families and visitors. One circuit of the outer square is about 400 m and takes 10 minutes. Three rounds at a slow pace, then tea on a rooftop as the lights come on, is our favourite way to end a Kathmandu day.

highlights.title: The stupa terraces
highlights.text: A gate on the north side lets you climb onto the stepped platforms of the stupa itself, where the dome rises directly above you and the square spreads out below. Walk clockwise here too. Prayer wheels set into the base wall, small carved images of the Buddha and the painted eyes are all close enough to study in detail.

highlights.title: Shechen and the monasteries
highlights.text: A short walk from the square, Shechen Monastery has a large prayer hall with painted walls and rows of young monks at their lessons. Many smaller gompas around the stupa welcome quiet visitors in the morning puja or the afternoon chanting. Remove shoes at the door, walk clockwise and never photograph monks without asking.

highlights.title: Thangka studios and craft shops
highlights.text: The lanes off the square are full of thangka workshops where painters grind mineral pigments and lay out deities on precise grids. Some paintings take months. You can watch the artists, buy a small work or sign up for a hands-on session, and nearby shops sell singing bowls, incense and Tibetan carpets.

highlights.title: Rooftop cafes facing the stupa
highlights.text: Several cafes on the ring of buildings around the square have terraces at eye level with the stupa's tower. Come for butter tea, momos and thukpa, or a coffee at dawn when pilgrims circle below and the light is soft. Rooftop tables near the edge fill first around sunset.

highlights.title: Losar and full-moon days
highlights.text: Tibetan New Year, Losar, usually falls in February or March and is the busiest time at Boudha, with new prayer flags raised, tsampa flour thrown in the air and families in their best clothes. Full-moon days through the year also draw large crowds and long rows of butter lamps.

how_to_reach.text: Boudhanath is about 6 km north-east of Thamel, 25 to 45 minutes by car depending on traffic at Chabahil. Taxis from Thamel cost about NPR 500 to 700, and our private vehicles drop you at the main gate on the Boudha road. Microbuses run from Ratna Park to Boudha for a few rupees, but they are crowded and stop often.

Tribhuvan International Airport is around 4 km away, about 15 minutes by car, so Boudha is a natural first stop on arrival day or a last visit before an evening flight. Several of our arrival itineraries end the first afternoon here with the evening kora, which also helps with jet lag.

From Pashupatinath the walk is about 2 km and 30 to 40 minutes, crossing the Mrigasthali forest and then following local lanes north to the stupa. We often combine the two on a single afternoon walk: Boudha first, then Pashupatinath for the evening aarti, or the reverse with the kora at dusk.

where_to_stay: Staying beside the stupa lets you walk the kora at dawn before the day trippers arrive and again after dark when the square is lit by lamps. Small guesthouses and family-run hotels line the lanes around the square, and a few monasteries offer simple rooms to visitors; quality varies, so we inspect before we book. Gokarna Forest Resort, about 15 to 20 minutes north-east by car, is our Premium choice for families who want space, forest walks and calm evenings near Boudha. Dwarika's Hotel in Battisputali, about 3 km south, is the most comfortable luxury option close by.
tips: Always walk clockwise around the stupa, the monasteries and any chorten, keeping them on your right.
Arrive by 6 am for the quietest kora and soft light, or after 5 pm for the busiest and most atmospheric one.
Keep your entry ticket with you, as staff at the gates may check it again on your way back into the square.
Dress modestly and remove shoes and hats before entering any gompa, and never step over a seated monk's robes or cushion.
Ask before photographing monks, nuns or people praying, and switch off the flash inside monastery halls.

experiences.title: Evening kora around Boudhanath stupa
experiences.best_time: 5–7 pm, all year; Oct–Mar for clear evenings
experiences.summary: A guided dusk walk with the Tibetan community around the Boudhanath stupa, three slow circuits of the square with time on the stupa terraces and a rooftop tea as the lamps are lit. Your guide explains prayer wheels, mantras and the symbolism of the stupa as you walk.
body: We meet at the main gate around 5 pm, or 4:30 pm in midwinter, when the shadows are long and the white dome turns gold. Your guide starts with the layout: the three terraces that form a mandala, the dome as the womb of the universe, the thirteen rings of the spire as steps toward enlightenment and the eyes looking out in all four directions. Then we join the kora, walking clockwise with the crowd at its own unhurried pace.

On the first circuit we stay on the outer ring, past the prayer wheels set into the wall and the shops selling incense and juniper. On the second we climb onto the stupa's terraces through the north gate, where the noise of the square drops away and you can see devotees doing full-length prostrations on wooden boards. On the third we step into a small gompa on the square for a few minutes of chanting, and look into the lamp house where hundreds of butter lamps burn.

We finish with tea or a light Tibetan supper on a rooftop facing the stupa, watching the kora continue below as the lights come on, around 6:30 pm in October. The walk covers about 1.5 km on flat paving, so it suits every age and fitness level. You are welcome to spin the prayer wheels with your right hand as you pass; locals appreciate visitors who join in respectfully. Allow 2 hours in total, plus dinner if you like.

faqs.q: What does kora mean at Boudhanath?
faqs.a: Kora is the Tibetan word for a devotional circuit around a sacred site, always walked clockwise so the stupa stays on your right. Buddhists believe each circuit builds merit, and many locals walk 3, 7 or 108 rounds while reciting mantras such as Om Mani Padme Hum. Visitors of any faith are welcome to walk with them.

faqs.q: How long does one kora around Boudhanath take?
faqs.a: One circuit of the outer square is about 400 m and takes around 10 minutes at the slow pace of the evening crowd. The circuit on the stupa's terraces is shorter. Most visitors walk three rounds in 30 to 40 minutes, then sit on a rooftop. Devoted pilgrims may spend hours walking many more.

faqs.q: Is Boudhanath open in the evening?
faqs.a: Yes. The square stays open into the evening and the kora continues after dark, with the stupa lit and butter lamps burning. Ticket booths staff the main gates during the day, and the terrace gate on the stupa itself closes earlier. Hours can change, so check current status before you travel.

experiences.title: Boudha monasteries and butter lamp offering
experiences.price_hint: ≈ ₹2,000 per person with guide; lamps by donation
experiences.summary: A morning visit to two or three working monasteries around Boudhanath, sitting in on chanting where it is allowed, followed by lighting butter lamps at a lamp house beside the stupa. It is a calm, respectful introduction to Tibetan Buddhist practice for families and pilgrims.
body: We start at about 7:30 am, when many monasteries around Boudha hold their morning puja. Our first stop is usually Shechen Monastery, a few minutes' walk from the square, where the main hall is painted floor to ceiling with deities and lineage masters and young monks recite texts to the beat of drums and long horns. Visitors sit quietly along the side wall. Your guide explains the Nyingma school, the role of the lamas and what the monks are chanting.

From there we visit one or two smaller gompas of other traditions, often a Kagyu or Sakya monastery tucked behind the stupa, so you can see how the art and rituals differ. In each, shoes come off at the door, you walk clockwise around the hall, and it is polite to leave a small donation of NPR 50 to 100 at the altar. If the monks invite you for butter tea, accept with both hands. Photography inside halls is often not allowed, and your guide will tell you where it is.

We finish at one of the lamp houses beside the stupa, where devotees light rows of small lamps for good fortune, healing or departed family. You can light a few lamps yourself for a modest donation, set your intention and add a prayer flag on the terrace if you wish. The whole visit takes about 3 hours on foot. It suits Buddhist and Hindu pilgrims alike, and children usually love the horns and drums.

faqs.q: Can visitors enter the monasteries around Boudhanath?
faqs.a: Yes, most monasteries around Boudha welcome quiet visitors, especially during the morning and afternoon pujas. Remove shoes and hats, walk clockwise inside the hall, sit along the wall rather than in the monks' rows and do not photograph without permission. A few halls close at lunchtime or during private ceremonies, and your guide will know which.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to light butter lamps at Boudhanath?
faqs.a: Lighting lamps is done by donation, and a few lamps cost only a small amount, from around NPR 10 to 50 each depending on the size. Families sponsoring large rows of 108 or 1,000 lamps for a special occasion pay more, arranged with the lamp house in advance. Your guide can help with the arrangement.

faqs.q: Is the monastery visit suitable for Hindu pilgrims from India?
faqs.a: Yes. Many Indian pilgrims include Boudhanath on the same day as Pashupatinath, and Buddhist sites in Nepal welcome visitors of all faiths. The Buddha is honoured in Hindu tradition too, and the lamp offering feels familiar to most Indian families. Vegetarian food is easy to find in the cafes around the stupa.

experiences.title: Thangka painting workshop in Boudha
experiences.best_time: Morning or early afternoon, all year
experiences.summary: A hands-on session with a working thangka painter in a studio near the Boudhanath stupa. You learn how the canvas is prepared, sketch a Buddha figure on the traditional grid and paint with mineral colours, then take your practice piece home.
body: Thangka is the Tibetan art of painting Buddhist deities on cotton, used for meditation and teaching, and Boudha has dozens of studios that train young painters for years before they work alone. Our session starts with a tour of the workshop: canvases stretched on wooden frames, primed with chalk and glue and polished smooth, and painters at work on pieces that will take weeks or months. Your teacher explains the strict proportions that every figure follows.

Then you pick up a pencil. On a small primed canvas you draw the measuring grid and sketch the head and face of the Buddha, learning why the eyes, ears and hands must fall exactly on certain lines. After a short break you mix colours from ground minerals and plant pigments with glue and water, and fill the background and robe with fine brushes. Most beginners complete a simple coloured study in the three hours; the teacher adds outlines if you wish.

Sessions run for one to four people, which keeps it personal, and the teacher speaks working English; your guide translates when needed. Children over ten who like drawing do well, and the slow, careful work is calming after a busy day of sightseeing. There is no pressure to buy, but if you would like a finished thangka, the studio will explain how to judge quality, from the fineness of the lines to the use of real gold.

faqs.q: Do I need painting experience for the thangka workshop?
faqs.a: No experience is needed. The teacher guides beginners step by step through the grid, the sketch and the colouring, and most people finish a small coloured study of the Buddha's face or figure in three hours. Those who already draw can attempt more detail. All materials, including pigments and brushes, are provided in the price.

faqs.q: How much does a real thangka cost in Kathmandu?
faqs.a: Prices range widely, from about NPR 3,000 for a small, simple student piece to several lakh rupees for a large master work with real gold and fine detail. The quality of line, the pigments used and the time taken decide the price. Ask the studio to explain each piece, and buy from studios where you can see painters at work.

faqs.q: Can we take a thangka home to India or abroad?
faqs.a: Yes, new thangkas bought from shops and studios can be carried home in your luggage. Ask for a receipt and roll the painting carefully in a tube rather than folding it. Antique religious art is a different matter and may need export clearance from Nepal's Department of Archaeology, so avoid anything sold as old.

faqs.q: What is the entry fee for Boudhanath Stupa?
faqs.a: Foreign visitors pay around NPR 400 at the gates, while SAARC nationals, including Indians, pay a lower fee and Nepalis enter free. The ticket covers the square and the stupa terraces. Fees are revised from time to time, so check current status before you travel. Keep the ticket handy, as it may be checked again.

faqs.q: What is the best time of day to visit Boudhanath?
faqs.a: Late afternoon to dusk is the best time, from around 5 pm, when the kora is busiest, the light turns warm and butter lamps are lit. Early morning from 6 am is quieter and good for photography. Midday is the least atmospheric, with fewer pilgrims and harsh light on the white dome.

faqs.q: Can you climb onto Boudhanath Stupa?
faqs.a: Yes, you can walk on the stepped terraces at the base of the stupa through a gate on the north side, during daytime hours. The dome and the tower are not open to climb. Walk clockwise on the terraces, as you would on the square below, and avoid sitting with your feet pointing at the stupa.

faqs.q: How much time do we need at Boudhanath?
faqs.a: Allow 1.5 to 2 hours for the kora, the terraces and a rooftop tea. Add 1 to 2 hours for a monastery visit or a thangka workshop. Many travellers spend a half day here and continue to Pashupatinath, which is 2 km away, for the evening aarti.

faqs.q: Which is better, Boudhanath or Swayambhunath?
faqs.a: They are different, so most people see both. Boudhanath is a flat, open square around a massive stupa and feels like a living Tibetan neighbourhood, best at dusk. Swayambhunath sits on a hilltop above the city with steep steps, monkeys, temples and a wide view, best in the early morning. With only half a day, we pick Boudha for atmosphere.

faqs.q: Why is Boudhanath important to Tibetan Buddhists?
faqs.a: Boudhanath lay on the old trade route between Tibet and the Kathmandu Valley, and Tibetan traders and pilgrims prayed here for centuries. After 1959, exiled Tibetans settled around the stupa and built monasteries of all the main schools, making Boudha one of the most important centres of Tibetan Buddhism outside Tibet. Many lamas teach here every winter.

Losar, the Tibetan New Year, follows the lunar calendar and usually falls in February or early March. The main celebrations at Boudha run for three days, with prayers, new prayer flags and families throwing tsampa flour on the third day. Dates move each year, so check current status before you travel and book hotels early.

Yes, very. The cafes and restaurants around the stupa serve plenty of vegetarian food, including vegetable and paneer momos, thukpa noodle soup, Tibetan bread, dal bhat and Indian dishes. Several monasteries discourage meat around their gates, and many Tibetan families eat vegetarian on full-moon days. Jain meals need advance notice.

faqs.q: Can we join a meditation course near Boudhanath?
faqs.a: Yes. Kopan Monastery, on the hill about 3 km north of the stupa, runs introductory courses in Buddhism and meditation for visitors through much of the year, from short programmes to its well-known month-long November course. Places fill early, and schedules change, so check current status before you travel. We arrange transfers and accommodation around your course dates.
